name: The Restoration That Made The House Darker
symptom: A restored or renovated old house whose interior door heads are now plain, with a patch of new plaster or a run of blocking above them where an operable transom used to be. The back rooms of the plan - the ones with one window or none - are noticeably darker and stiller than the front. The owners say the house 'has always been dark', and the photographic and physical evidence says it was not.

cause.explanation: Three separate modern requirements all point at the transom. Fire and smoke separation between a dwelling and an attached garage, between storeys at a stair enclosure, and between dwelling units in a conversion each ask for a rated assembly, and a glazed opening over a door is the first thing a plan reviewer marks. Air conditioning then removes the transom's ventilation argument, because a conditioned house wants a sealed room and a return path through a grille rather than through a hole above a door. Privacy and sound, which the transom always compromised, finish the job. The result is a device removed for four defensible reasons by four people none of whom was thinking about light.
cause.cost_saved: $300-$800 per opening to close a transom, against $900-$2,200 to restore or reproduce one with its operating hardware.

rule_violated.statement: When a plan goes double-pile the back room loses its window wall and is lit through a door, a transom, a borrowed light or a single gable-end window, and the depth it can carry collapses to about 1.2 times the head height. The transom over an interior door is not a decorative motif; it is the device that made this room habitable, and removing it in a renovation is why so many restored double-pile houses feel dark in a way the owners cannot account for.
A transom over every interior door, with operable windows on both side walls of every room. The section is the cooling system.

A 24 by 36 in transom at a 7 ft head above a door delivers useful illuminance about 8 to 10 ft into the room beyond, which is the whole depth of a second-rank room. Nothing else in the wall does this, because a door is shut and a wall is opaque.

correct_practice: Treat the interior transom as structure of the daylight system rather than as trim. Where the historic fabric shows one - and the evidence is a wide head casing, a run of blocking, a ghost line in the plaster, or hinges and a rod in the attic of the trim - restore it operable. Sizes: transom light 12 to 24 in high over a 6 ft 8 in to 7 ft door head, glazed with a single light or a two- or three-light pattern matching the room's sash; hung on a centre pivot or a bottom-hinged hopper with a rod and a catch, because the whole point is that it opens. Where a rated separation genuinely applies - a garage wall, a stair enclosure, a demised party wall - use a rated glazed assembly or wired-look ceramic in a rated frame rather than blocking the opening, which costs more and preserves the room. Where a new transom is being introduced into new work, the rule is that any room deeper than about 1.2 times its head height and lit on one side only needs a second aperture, and a transom is the cheapest one available.

fixes.right: Reinstate the transom operable, with its rod and catch, glazed to match the room's sash pattern.
fixes.cheap: Reinstate it fixed. A fixed glazed transom recovers all of the light and none of the ventilation, costs $350-$700, and is reversible; where a rated assembly is required, a 20-minute rated glazed transom unit is $900-$1,600 and is still cheaper than the room being unusable. Where the head height is genuinely gone, a full-height glazed door panel or a sidelight beside the door recovers most of the borrowed light at the wrong height, which is worth having.
fixes.dishonest: A solid panel painted to look like a transom, or a mirrored one. It restores the elevation of the door and none of its function, and it is the exact move that persuades a later owner the house never had light in that room.

detection: Measure the head casing of the interior doors. A door casing that is unusually deep at the head, or a head that sits 12 to 24 in below a cornice with a blank panel between, indicates a filled transom. In an attic or a closet, look for the transom sash itself, which is very often stored on site. In a photograph of a hall, compare the door head height to the ceiling: an eighteenth or nineteenth-century door head at 6 ft 8 in under a 10 ft ceiling almost certainly had something over it. The functional detection is simpler: if a room off a hall has one window or none and reads dark, and the door head is blank, the transom has gone.

test.note: The limit for a room lit on one side by a single window, a borrowed light or a transom. Above 1.2 the room needs the transom; the fault is present when the room exceeds it and the transom has been removed.

exceptions.why: First Period interiors have no interior transoms; the rooms are small, the ceilings are 6 ft 8 in to 7 ft 6 in, and there is no head height for one. Adding transoms to a First Period house is the opposite anachronism.
exceptions.bounds: Only where the ceiling is genuinely under about 8 ft. A Georgianised First Period house with 8 ft 6 in ceilings and a passage may well have had them.

exceptions.why: Same reason: 7 ft to 7 ft 6 in ceilings leave no room over a door.
exceptions.bounds: Ceiling under 8 ft. Above that the type has been stretched and the transom question returns.

exceptions.why: The Craftsman interior uses a continuous plate rail and a high frieze band rather than transoms, and the wide cased opening does the borrowing instead - the opening between living and dining is a permanent transom the width of the room.
exceptions.bounds: Requires the wide cased openings actually to be there. A Craftsman bungalow with narrow doors and no transoms and no cased openings is dark for the ordinary reason.

exceptions.why: The continuous high lintel band of art-glass casements raises the head across every exterior wall, so interior borrowing is not the strategy.
exceptions.bounds: Requires the continuous lintel band returning round every corner without interruption.

confused_with.difference: That is an exterior door's transom bar and a proportion fault on the elevation. This is an interior transom and a daylight fault in the plan; they share a word and nothing else.
That is the geometry. This is the loss of the historical remedy for it, and it is the one that gets committed by people trying to do the right thing.

severity_by_style.why: A transom over every interior door is a hard constraint of the type; without them a 40 ft deep single-file plan has two apertures for five rooms and the section stops working.
The stack ventilation depends on high openings; a blocked transom traps the hot air the tall room was built to exhaust.
No head height for a transom to begin with.

severity_trajectory: Minor at the moment of the work and serious permanently afterwards, because it is very rarely reversed: once the head is plastered flat and a cornice or a fire assembly runs across it, the next owner has no evidence the transom existed and inherits the darkness as a fact about old houses.
